content.comment_body: I installed the unit about four years ago. It operates the outputs daily, so it's switched roughly 1500 times, which isn't much for a typical quality relay. Over time, three relays have become stuck on—one relay failed around two years back and the other two within the last few months. The connected loads weren't excessive: for one, there were six 7W compact fluorescent lamps; for another, two 50W halogen bulbs; and for the last, five 7W LED lamps. These loads are all well below the stated 3A/10A rating. This suggests the relays may not be of optimal quality. Is this issue common for the 230V models? Does anyone know which specific relay is used inside the module? I don't have access right now, but I'm considering swapping the relay with a different manufacturer's type since I assume warranty is no longer valid.

It's straightforward to open the unit. If you press the plastic tabs on both sides, you can easily remove the rear cover, and then the lower circuit board comes out. This exposes the relays so you can check the manufacturer's details and type number. Keep in mind, opening the unit voids the warranty with [company_name]. Considering the time, effort, and cost of replacing four relays, it may be more economical to buy a new unit.

I realize opening the module is simple, but I don't have it nearby right now so I'm looking to prepare ahead. On the other hand, buying a new device isn't practical if the relays only last two to four years with modest use and low power loads, which seems like an unacceptably high failure rate. Unless they've improved later versions, replacing the faulty relays with another brand through soldering seems like the best approach.
The module in question contains four relays from SCHRACK, model V23061-A1007-A302, with a 24VDC coil.

Hello, Relay failures here aren't necessarily due to poor quality. LED and energy-saving lamps on 230V AC are capacitive loads. When switching these, the inrush current can be over 100 times greater than the normal operating current. Such high inrush current can damage relay contacts. Components designed to limit the inrush current are recommended for these types of lamps. I hope this clarifies the situation.

analysis.insight_summary: Users are experiencing unexpected relay failures in a specific module, even when operating well below the rated load and with relatively few switching cycles. Questions are being raised about the long-term reliability and suitability of the relays, especially when used with modern lamp types, and concerns have been voiced about whether the product is robust enough for capacitive loads.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect the relays in this module to function reliably for several years and thousands of cycles under moderate, rated loads, without early failure. Reliable operation with current lighting technologies—such as LEDs and compact fluorescent lamps—is also anticipated.
